Αρχικά, απαιτείται από τον θεατή να αποδεχτεί και να θεωρήσει ως φυσιολογικές τις κατ’ εξακολούθηση απιθανότητες της πλοκής. Όλοι βρίσκονται βολικά στο σωστό μέρος, τη σωστή στιγμή για να μπορέσει να εξελιχθεί η ιστορία. Ταυτόχρονα, έξτρα challenge προσδίδει και το ακατανόητο μοντάζ που μόνο περισσότερο δυσνόητο και κουραστικό έκανε το σενάριο. Και το κερασάκι στην τούρτα: τα ανόητα plot twists που είναι τελικά και ο αυτοσκοπός της ταινίας. Η πλοκή μοιάζει να λειτουργεί επειδή ο σεναριογράφος πρέπει να την κάνει εκβιαστικά να λειτουργήσει, και όχι επειδή οι χαρακτήρες θα μπορούσαν ρεαλιστικά να οδηγηθούν εκεί. Για να φτάσουμε, τελικά, σε χαζούς εντυπωσιασμούς και ανατροπές. Ουαου. Τίποτα δεν δικαιολογεί την πολυπλοκότητα της ταινίας σε ένα πιο ουσιώδες επίπεδο, αλλά αντίθετα όλο αυτό το ατελείωτο δίωρο εξυπηρετεί μόνο τη λύση ενός γρίφου με παιδικές εξηγήσεις. Τέλος, οι γυναικείοι χαρακτήρες λειτουργούν ως παθητικοί αποδέκτες στις πράξεις των πρωταγωνιστών( με εξαίρεση ίσως τον ρόλο της Scarlett Johnsson), ενώ  δυστυχώς ο ρόλος του Bowie καταλήγει ως μια ωραία ιδέα κάστινγκ και τίποτα περισσότερο. Το μόνο που δίνω είναι ότι σου εξηγεί την μαγεία και όλα αυτά τα τρικ, και την ίδια στιγμή κάνει μια προσπάθεια να ξεγελάσει και εσένα ως θεατή. Le film — ou plutôt les critiques — m'ont bien dupé. Mais qu'est-ce que c'est que cette bouse, sérieusement ?! Comme d'habitude avec Christopher Nolan, il n'est pas vraiment réalisateur mais plutôt écrivain : il passe son temps à expliquer ce qui se passe à l'écran au lieu de nous laisser le découvrir par nous-mêmes. Déjà, je crois que je n'ai jamais vu un plot twist aussi ridicule de ma vie. Si je résume globalement l'histoire : des magiciens trouvent comme par magie des doubles d'eux-mêmes et les tuent. Voilà donc l'incroyable chef-d'œuvre dont tout le monde me parlait. C'est du foutage de gueule. Comme d'hab, Nolan nous balance son projet sans réelle construction. Il utilise ses personnages comme décor et son décor comme personnage. Tout est artificiel et prétentieux. Le film se croit incroyablement intelligent et intellectuel alors qu'il nous propose énormément de choses absurdes. Le jeu d'acteur, les dialogues complètement débiles, les rebondissements qui s'enchaînent avec un ridicule alarmant... Tout semble vouloir nous prouver à quel point le film est intelligent, sans réellement réussir à le démontrer. Et puis le film passe son putain de temps à tuer tout le monde au lieu de réellement nous balancer de la magie. Maintenant, si tuer des personnes et faire apparaître des doubles, c'est ça la magie, mieux vaut que je ne dise rien. L'histoire est complètement tirée par les cheveux, parfois même nanardesque. Et même la présentation du film est mensongère : on nous vend quelque chose de mystérieux et spectaculaire, alors qu'on se retrouve surtout devant un mélodrame surjoué avec des acteurs en double, présentés comme si c'était le miracle du siècle. Et le pire, c'est cette impression de recyclage permanent. Le film reprend des idées déjà vues auparavant et nous ressort exactement le même délire de merde que dans Inception : un concept compliqué, une narration qui veut absolument paraître intelligente et des explications qui prennent le dessus sur l'émotion et le spectacle. Et on va vraiment me dire que ce film est captivant ?! Je préfère regarder des films sous-cotés. Au moins, je suis sûr de ne pas être déçu, parce que les chers cinéphiles me conseillent des grosses daubes qui servent strictement à rien. Bon, tout n'est pas à jeter. Les passages avec Tesla sont probablement parmi les plus intéressants, notamment lorsqu'on découvre le fonctionnement de certaines expériences. Le développement des règles du tour de magie est également plutôt bien construit : le film respecte finalement assez bien l'idée qu'un tour doit avoir un principe, une méthode et une réparation derrière lui. Mais à part ça... Tout est digne d'un film qui se fout royalement de votre gueule. Un film qui se croit intelligent alors qu'il ne l'est pas. Un film qui te balance des rebondissements totalement débiles à chaque scène. Et cette fin... C'est clairement le complot poussé jusqu'au ridicule le plus alarmant. J'étais à deux doigts de l'arêter avant la fin... Nolan n'a décidément pas fini de me décevoir. Mais bon, je regarderai quand même ses autres films ultérieurement... De la merde...

This is definitionally High Camp but because it somehow pertains to straight male culture it is not considered as such and that friction is a big part of why our culture’s usage of the word camp pisses me off but that’s a different subject. The opening shot being the cemetery of top hats, I instantly cackled! And then winced because the sound effects where so loud but the dialogue barely audible! How are you meant to watch this without subtitles?! What I think is fascinating is truly how every aspect of this film exemplifies the idea of failed seriousness but because it was made by a posh autistic British man we are meant to think of it as elevated. The way it tells you the plot in the first minute (and also that it follows a very classic narrative three part act because that’s what films are!), the performances and the accents are insanely over the top, the terrible wigs and prosthetic hair pieces, it’s all just very silly. But it treats this silliness with the utmost seriousness which I think is really funny but it also saps any Levity out of it. It’s a dour, very heavy handed drama for Harry Potter adults that, ironically for the subject matter, almost compulsively tells rather than shows you. I think there is something inherently so telling about choosing to make a film about prestidigitation where all magic is “logical” or at least scientific. Because those type of magicians are ontologically opposed to the idea of natural magic, predicated on the need for explanation. I think this film prefigures so much of the current horrors with its damn flashbacks, the way everyone constantly announces their intentions and how women are nothing but plot contrivances (Rebecca Hall you deserved better than this and the second you appeared on screen I instantly got sad for the unceremonious way you were ineluctably doomed to get fridged) I think I will just never understand why people revere Nolan, I find his filmmaking so clunky and laden footed and I can’t really understand this obsession with making everything so self serious even though you pick quite silly themes or subjects but hey! I guess I’m just left with how much I loathe how Christian Bale holds his mouth in this and I could never see anything else in his scenes

Their actions carry no weight because there was no established ground for them to be based off of. They exist for the sole purpose of spouting corny one liners and making the most retarded and nonsensical decisions just to force the plot in the direction that Nolan wants. None of the events that happened evoke any sort of emotion in me besides being frustrated at how stupid and nonsensical all the characters are. So instead of these ideas being given the proper time and care to be fleshed out and explored, they get buried under the countless cheesy one-liners and stupidly and forcibly convoluted plotlines, to the point where they become unrecognisable by the end of the movie. When I finished it, I had no idea what was I supposed to get out of it, and after sitting on it, I'm even more confused. It all got sacrificed for the sake of setting up the plot twists at the end, which served nothing but be plot twists for the sake of being plot twists. If anything, they made the story worse. You needn't think for more than five seconds to recognise how stupid the ending is. The movie would've worked much better as a comedy rather than a cat-and-mouse-chase-esque thriller. Una vez más, se trata el tema de la obsesión y de querer ser el mejor o el más reconocido en un ámbito. Y, como ya es sabido, estos comportamientos no suelen acabar bien. A partir de ahí, es un sinfín de manipulaciones el uno al otro, hasta que llega a su fin de un modo u otro. Centrándome un poco en la narrativa, a pesar de haber visto este recurso anteriormente de manera continua, siento que a esta película en concreto le viene muy bien. The Good This was only my second watch, and I was impressed to find I liked it even more this time. The first time you watch The Prestige, Nolan pulls off a fantastic trick. He places the audience in essentially the same position as Angier. You become fascinated by Borden's secret because Angier is fascinated by it, and Nolan controls what you see and when you see it beautifully. And the reveal works so well, with the cost of obsession and sacrifice hitting all at once. The second time, the balance almost reverses. The ending may not hit the same, but the rest of the film works even better. You know the cost from the beginning, and suddenly every interaction is carrying something it couldn't quite carry the first time around. You’re watching Angier’s grief, bitterness and obsession knowing exactly where it's going to take him, and Hugh Jackman is fantastic here. There’s a desperation to him that develops so gradually that you can see him disappearing into it. But it's Borden who changed most for me on a second watch. Knowing his secret means you can see the cost of it written across virtually every interaction. Borden and Fallon, Borden and Sarah, the moments of apparent inconsistency, the distance, the things he can and can't remember, even the moments of genuine love followed by something that suddenly feels completely different. None of this was absent the first time. The reveal makes you understand it retrospectively. On a second watch, you get to live with it as it's happening. And there’s a wonderful symmetry between the two men. Borden gives up an entire life for the trick and can never let anybody know. Angier ultimately does something even more horrifying, all in pursuit of a version of the trick that, to the audience watching it, isn’t actually any better. That’s the beautiful punchline. He can finally be the man who appears at the back of the theatre and takes the applause himself. That’s it. Nobody in the crowd knows or cares what he had to do to achieve it. The difference only matters to Angier. Both men have sacrificed everything for something whose true cost can never be appreciated by the people applauding them. The Bad We’re scraping around here. One thing that bothered me slightly was Borden insisting that he doesn’t know which knot he tied when Julia died. Obviously, once you know the secret, there’s an explanation for why one Borden genuinely might not know. But surely the brothers talked about it? It’s such a monumental event in both their lives that the idea they could maintain uncertainty between themselves feels a little difficult to swallow. There’s perhaps an interesting reading where their identities have become so blurred that even responsibility is becoming shared between them, but I’m not entirely convinced the film earns that. There’s also some fairly aggressive plot convenience around Borden being convicted of Angier’s murder. He’s found at the scene, certainly, and Angier has constructed the situation to incriminate him, but everyone becomes awfully confident awfully quickly that Borden murdered him. In a film absolutely stuffed with doubles, deception, disappearing men and people whose entire profession involves making things appear to happen that didn’t, there isn’t a great deal of appetite for another explanation. It works because the plot needs it to work. And the meh... This was my second watch, and it leaves me wondering what happens on the third. The first time is a marvel, the second is richer. So what does a third watch give me? I had a similar thought after revisiting Inception. There’s always the possibility that once you've experienced the revelation and then experienced the film again with that knowledge, you've exhausted the major ways it can change beneath you. But my suspicion with The Prestige is that it will keep giving, because it's simply too rich beneath the mechanics of its trick. The secret isn't a replacement for the human story. It's the thing that reveals just how much of that human story Nolan had hidden in plain sight. And second time around, I could see it everywhere.

The Prestige is easily Christopher Nolan’s most underrated film. Not underrated in the sense that people think it’s bad but rather that it tends to be overshadowed by his other films like The Dark Knight, Interstellar and Inception. From a character perspective, The Prestige may be Nolan’s most complicated films. The complexity and the rivalry between Angier and Borden is the film’s main point of interest and both Hugh Jackman and Christian Bale nail their performances. The ensemble and supporting cast all does a terrific job but it’s the two leads that truly stand out. Every aspect of the movie draws you deeper into the story and the twist at the end feels realistic and earned. Like any Nolan film, the narrative structure jumps around the story’s timeline and in this film specifically runs the risk of becoming overly complex and confusing. The editing, however, is, dare I say, perfect. Instead of being the confusing mess it could have been, The Prestige effortlessly jumps around the timeline and feels natural while doing so. It’s not going to be my favorite Nolan film (although it may easily become the one I enjoy rewatching the most) but The Prestige is a masterpiece.

🍃Everything about this held up on a rewatch. I love how uncharacteristically (Nolan-wise) gritty this was. The London streets feel grimy and atmospheric while they host our main characters in an inescapable feedback loop of ambition and depravity. Bale’s performance is just unreal on a rewatch. The subtle physicality and expression work done to distinguish between the twins is crazy work. Jackman is also great, giving one of his best performances. The entire supporting ensemble is similarly excellent. The Root stuff stretches credibility for me and there is a moment halfway where the film feels slightly repetitive but I remained completely engrossed.

Nolan is a master at twists, not because they’re surprising or obvious but because they’re both.  He lays breadcrumbs that lets the viewer figure it out before the big reveal, but it’s subtle enough so that when it is shown the buildup still carries the weight.  This movie is no different.  It’s essentially Spy vs Spy but they’re both asshole magicians and its amazing.
